plain_definition: The price at the end of a trading day. Each candle has one close. It is the price most people look at.
example: If the close on day 10 is 104 and on day 11 is 106, the price went up.

plain_definition: The price at the start of a trading day.
example: A candle that opens at 100 and closes at 103 is an up day.

plain_definition: The highest and lowest prices reached during one day. They are the thin lines above and below a candle.
example: High 108 and low 99 means the price moved between 99 and 108 that day.

plain_definition: One box on the chart that shows one day. It shows where the price started, where it ended, and how far it went up and down in between.
example: A tall candle means a day with a big move.

plain_definition: One trading day, counted from 1. We show 'Day 87' instead of a real date, so you cannot guess the year.
example: Day 60 is the day you can see today. Day 61 is tomorrow.

plain_definition: How many days ahead your guess looks. With a horizon of 5, you guess if the price in 5 days will be higher than today.
example: On day 60, a guess with horizon 5 is answered on day 65.

plain_definition: How likely something is, from 0% (never) to 100% (always). If you say 70% ten times, you should be right about seven times.
example: 70% means: I am fairly sure, but not certain.

plain_definition: Your answer to one question: will the price be higher in a few days? You also say how sure you are. You cannot change a guess after you send it.
example: I am 60% sure the price will be higher in 5 days.

plain_definition: A score for guesses made with percentages. Lower is better and zero is perfect. Saying 50% every time scores 0.25, so a score below 0.25 beats a coin flip.
example: A score of 0.23 is a little better than guessing. A score of 0.30 is worse.

plain_definition: Saying 50% every time. It always scores 0.25. This is the line to beat before you can say you did better than guessing.
example: If your score is 0.27, a coin flip would have done better.

plain_definition: Calibration asks: when you said 70%, did it happen about 7 times out of 10? Good calibration means your confidence matches how often you are right.
example: Dots on the diagonal line of the plot mean you were well calibrated.

plain_definition: How often something happens in general. If prices rise on 53 of 100 days, the base rate for 'up' is 53%. Start your thinking there.
example: With a base rate of 53%, saying 50% is already close to the truth.

plain_definition: A good score can happen by chance. The luck check mixes up the answers many times and counts how often random answers score as well as you did.
example: If random answers match your score 4 times in 10, your score may be luck.

plain_definition: A stretch of price history with the name, the dates and the price level hidden. You only see 'Day 1, Day 2, ...', so you cannot rely on memory.
example: You do not know if it is a famous year or a made-up chart.

plain_definition: The moment you find out what the episode really was. It ends the episode. Guesses that are still waiting will not be counted.
example: After the reveal you see the stock name and the real dates.

plain_definition: A price chart made by a random-number program. It looks real, but no one can predict it. It shows how easy it is to see patterns in noise.
example: If you do well on made-up charts, it was luck.

plain_definition: How many answers a score is based on. A score from 10 guesses can change a lot. We wait for 30 answers before saying anything.
example: Ten coin flips can give 8 heads. A thousand almost never do.

plain_definition: Feeling more sure than you should. If you say 90% but are right only 6 times out of 10, you are overconfident.
example: Many people say 90% when they are right about 70% of the time.

plain_definition: The feeling, after you know what happened, that it was easy to see coming. Blind episodes avoid this by hiding the outcome.
example: After a crash, people say 'the signs were clear'. Before it, they were not.

plain_definition: Where the numbers came from: who supplied them, when they were saved, and how they were adjusted. We show it after the reveal.
example: Prices were adjusted for splits as of the last day you saw.

plain_definition: How busy trading was compared with the first days you saw. A value of 1 means as busy as at the start. A value of 2 means twice as busy.
example: Relative volume 0.5 is a quiet day.

plain_definition: In a blind chart the first price is always shown as 100. Only the changes matter. A price of 110 means 10% higher than at the start.
example: Price 95 means 5% lower than the first day.

plain_definition: Looking only at companies that still exist today. The ones that failed are missing, so results can look better than they really were.
example: A list of today's big stocks leaves out the ones that went bust.

plain_definition: Guesses that look at the same days. A 10-day guess made each day shares most of its days with the next one, so they are not fully independent.
example: Ten guesses in a row may count as fewer than ten pieces of evidence.

plain_definition: A clear instruction for when to buy and when to sell. A computer can follow it without any guessing.
example: Buy when the short average is above the long average. Sell when it is not.

plain_definition: The average price over the last few days. Each day it moves forward by one day. It smooths out the daily ups and downs.
example: The 20-day average on day 30 uses the prices from day 11 to day 30.

plain_definition: The moment when a short average moves above or below a long average. Many simple rules use this moment to buy or sell.
example: The 20-day average rises above the 100-day average. The rule buys.

plain_definition: The older part of a stock's history. You may try as many rules on it as you like. The newest years are locked in the vault.
example: About 17 years of practice and 4 years in the vault.

plain_definition: The newest years of a stock's history, locked away. You can open it once, for one rule. Then you see how that rule did on years it never saw.
example: You try 20 rules on the practice years, then open the vault with your favourite.

plain_definition: Each different rule you run on the practice years counts as one idea tried. Running the exact same rule again does not count twice.
example: Rules 5/20 and 10/40 are two ideas. Running 5/20 again is still two.

plain_definition: A chart where every line starts at 100. If a line ends at 187, then 100 turned into 187. It makes two lines easy to compare.
example: The rule ends at 150 and buy and hold ends at 210.

plain_definition: A way to draw the up-and-down axis so that equal percent changes look equal. Without it, the last years of a long chart look far bigger.
example: A rise from 100 to 110 looks as tall as a rise from 1,000 to 1,100.

plain_definition: The biggest drop from a high point to a later low point. It shows how much a holder had to sit through.
example: A worst fall of 30% means 100 fell to 70 at some point.

plain_definition: The steady yearly rate that would give the same end result. It lets you compare windows of different length.
example: 100 turning into 250 in 10 years is about 9.6% a year.

plain_definition: The share of days when the rule held the stock. Buy and hold is in the stock almost every day.
example: 56% means the rule was invested on 56 days out of 100.

plain_definition: Made-up price histories built by shuffling blocks of the real daily moves. They show how often luck alone does as well as your rule.
example: If 40 of 100 mixed-up histories do as well, your result is not special.

plain_definition: A run of the same result in a row, such as seven heads when flipping a coin. Streaks often come from luck alone.
example: In 100 coin flips, a run of 6 or 7 heads is normal.

plain_definition: A test of a rule on past prices. It shows what the rule would have done, not what it will do.
example: We ran the rule on 2005 to 2021 prices and compared it with buy and hold.
